title: Haggai
subtitle: Chaggai, “Festive”
description: The tenth of the twelve Minor Prophets: four short messages, each dated to the day, given in 520 BC to the exiles who had come home from Babylon and left the LORD’s house in ruins while they panelled their own. “Think carefully about how you are living,” Haggai tells them: you have sown much and harvested little, and earned wages only “to put them in a purse with holes.” Unusually for a prophet, he was heeded at once. To builders discouraged by how small the new temple looked he brought the word “I am with you”, the promise that its glory would be greater than Solomon’s, and a signet ring for Zerubbabel. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Haggai about?
qa.answer: The rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem after the exile. The Jews who returned from Babylon had laid its foundation and then stopped, saying the time had not come. In four dated messages Haggai calls them to rebuild (1:1–15), encourages them when the new house looks like nothing beside Solomon’s (2:1–9), teaches that holiness is not passed on by contact while uncleanness is, and promises blessing from that day on (2:10–19), and declares that God has chosen Zerubbabel as his signet ring (2:20–23).

qa.question: When did Haggai prophesy?
qa.answer: All four of his messages are dated to the second year of King Darius I of Persia, 520 BC: the first day of the sixth month, the twenty-first day of the seventh, and the twenty-fourth day of the ninth, twice. The book of Ezra records that Haggai and Zechariah prophesied together and that the people, encouraged by them, finished the temple in the sixth year of Darius, 515 BC (Ezra 5:1; 6:14–15). Nothing else is known of Haggai’s life.

qa.question: What does “Think carefully about how you are living” mean in Haggai?
qa.answer: It renders a Hebrew idiom, literally “set your heart on your ways”, which older Bibles translate “consider your ways” (1:5, 1:7). Haggai asks the people to look at the results of their priorities: they have sown much and harvested little, eaten and not been satisfied, and earned wages only to put them in a purse with holes, because they have built their own houses and neglected the LORD’s.

qa.question: How would the glory of the second temple be greater than the first?
qa.answer: The returned exiles thought their temple looked like nothing compared with Solomon’s (2:3). God promised to shake the nations and fill it with glory, so that “The glory of this house in the future will be greater than its glory in the past” (2:9). Christians have understood this as fulfilled when Jesus came to that temple and taught in its courts, and more widely in the church as the dwelling of God; Hebrews 12:26–28 reads Haggai’s promise to shake heaven and earth as pointing to the final kingdom that cannot be shaken.

qa.question: Why is Zerubbabel called a signet ring?
qa.answer: A signet ring was a ruler’s seal, his authority worn on his hand. Jeremiah had told King Jehoiachin (Coniah), Zerubbabel’s grandfather, that even if he were the signet ring on God’s right hand, God would pull him off (Jeremiah 22:24). Haggai 2:23 reverses that word for Zerubbabel, renewing God’s choice of David’s line. Zerubbabel was a governor, not a king, but he appears in the family line of Jesus in Matthew 1 and Luke 3, and Christians read the promise as reaching its goal in Christ.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.
